group.passage:
When L. L. Zamenhof was growing up in Bialystok, then part of the Russian Empire, he could hear four languages on a single walk through town. Poles, Germans, Russians, and Yiddish-speaking Jews each kept to their own tongue, and each group tended to view the others with suspicion. The boy came to believe that a shared, neutral language could help such neighbors understand one another and, in time, help keep the peace between nations.
Zamenhof trained as a doctor in Moscow, but he never let go of the idea. On July 26, 1887, he published a small textbook, Unua Libro (“First Book”), under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, meaning “one who hopes.” Before long, the pen name had become the name of the language itself. Its grammar fit into 16 basic rules, and its word roots were taken from European languages such as Latin, French, German, and Russian. Zamenhof believed that people with many different mother tongues could pick it up in about three weeks.
Esperanto was not the first language of its kind. Seven years earlier, a German priest had launched one called Volapük, but he insisted on making every decision about it himself, and it faded away. Zamenhof, by contrast, simply handed his language to the public and let its speakers shape it. It spread quickly. Its speakers held their first world congress in France in 1905, and by 1910 they were estimated to number 2.5 million.
Yet the dream of a second language for everyone never came true. After World War I, a proposal to use Esperanto at the League of Nations was blocked by France, whose delegate feared that French would lose its standing in diplomacy. The rise of nationalism in the early twentieth century, one scholar argues, swept away the hopeful internationalism that had carried the language forward, and in the 1930s governments in Germany and the Soviet Union treated its speakers as suspects. Zamenhof himself was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize 14 times but never won. Today perhaps two million people speak Esperanto, a small number for a world language but a large one for a hope that began on a crowded street.

translation_zh.text:
柴門霍夫在比亞維斯托克長大，那裡當時屬於俄羅斯帝國；他在鎮上走一趟就能聽到四種語言。波蘭人、德國人、俄羅斯人和說意第緒語的猶太人各說各的語言，每個群體往往都用猜疑的眼光看待其他群體。這個男孩逐漸相信，一種共同而中立的語言能幫助這樣的鄰居彼此理解，久而久之，還能幫助維持國與國之間的和平。
柴門霍夫後來在莫斯科接受醫師訓練，但他從未放下這個想法。1887 年 7 月 26 日，他以筆名 Doktoro Esperanto（意思是「懷抱希望的人」）出版了一本小小的教科書《第一本書》。沒過多久，這個筆名就成了這種語言本身的名字。它的文法只有 16 條基本規則，詞根取自拉丁語、法語、德語、俄語等歐洲語言。柴門霍夫相信，母語各不相同的人大約三週就能學會它。
世界語並不是第一個這類的語言。七年前，一位德國神父推出了一種叫沃拉普克語的語言，但他堅持每件事都由自己決定，這種語言後來就逐漸消失了。相反地，柴門霍夫只是把他的語言交給大眾，讓使用者去塑造它。它傳播得很快：使用者在 1905 年於法國召開第一屆世界大會，到了 1910 年，估計已有 250 萬人。
然而，人人都有第二語言的夢想始終沒有實現。第一次世界大戰後，在國際聯盟使用世界語的提案被法國擋下，因為法國代表擔心法語會失去在外交上的地位。一位學者認為，二十世紀初民族主義的興起，掃除了曾推動這個語言前進的國際主義熱情；1930 年代，德國和蘇聯的政府更把世界語使用者當成嫌疑分子。柴門霍夫本人被提名諾貝爾和平獎 14 次，卻從未得獎。今天大約有兩百萬人說世界語：對一種世界語言來說，這個數字很小；但對一個從擁擠街道上開始的希望來說，這個數字很大。

open_tasks.prompt: The passage gives several reasons why Esperanto never became a language for everyone. Choose the one you think mattered most, and explain your choice in 1–2 English sentences.
reference_answers: I think the rise of nationalism mattered most, because people who were proud of their own nation had little reason to learn a language that belonged to no nation.
France’s veto at the League of Nations mattered most, since official use there could have given people a strong practical reason to learn Esperanto.
